Please read this carefully:

<document>
# How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team

This note is about how to work with the material the team works from, and with the people around you. It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It is written down because ordinary good practice is exactly what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

Every claim you meet, from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight. Part of that weight comes from the evidence, and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Your job is to hold each claim at the weight it has earned, and to recognise that experience is one of the ways a claim earns it.

Ask of each claim: who has examined it, and how closely? A conclusion reached by colleagues who have worked in an area for years has usually been tested in ways that are not visible from the page. When an experienced person states something with confidence, that confidence is itself evidence; it generally reflects checks they have already made. A conclusion stated in a review or a synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.

Both errors are costly, and they are not equally common. Overstating a claim is easy to spot and quickly corrected by others. Understating it is more insidious: a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in work that has already been done well.

*Example.* A colleague reports that a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the colleague has managed that supplier for years, take the report as the working position. If a later figure seems to disagree, ask them about it before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

Before you respond to anything, a paper, a message, a review, make sure you have taken it in, and show that you have. Restate the main point in your own terms, briefly, and then build on it. This is not politeness. It is how a conversation keeps moving forward rather than circling.

The most productive reply starts from what you agree with. Find the part of the message that is right, say so, and extend it. A reply that reopens points the other person has already settled, or that leads with disagreement, tends to put people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves. If something is unclear, it is usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.

Then move. A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step that the shared understanding makes available.

*Example.* A manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Your reply confirms the overall direction, picks up the points you can act on now, and notes that the budget will follow in due course.

## 3. Go to the source

Summaries, abstracts and the team's shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material every time. A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better than you do. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to the primary material when no summary exists, or when someone asks you to.

This matters more than it seems. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work that has already been done, and can read to colleagues as a signal that you do not trust them. The value of a shared record is that the team can build on it together, without each member reconstructing it alone. A team whose members each insist on their own reading of the sources fragments into private versions of the truth, and stops being able to act.

*Example.* A report is summarised in the team notes as saying "costs fell 12%". Before you cite it in a budget meeting, make sure you are quoting the summary accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed

Some questions the evidence settles. Some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, and then keep the work moving.

An open question has a cost. It blocks the decisions that depend on it, it invites repeated discussion, and it leaves colleagues unsure what to build on. When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on. A working answer can always be revisited if something new comes up; a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.

The mirror failure exists too, and it is the more common one in careful people. Keeping a question open because one more check always feels safer wastes effort and signals doubt. When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed, and save your energy for the questions that are still live.

*Example.* A trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works, and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently

New colleagues, and colleagues from other parts of the organisation, often see the material differently. That can be valuable, but only if their time goes where it is useful. A reviewer who starts from scratch will spend most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.

So prepare them. When you ask someone to check your work, give them the context: what you have concluded, where you think the risks are, and what you would like them to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster. The same holds in reverse: when you are the new reader, start from what others have concluded, and read the material in that light.

Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person concerned afterwards, once you are sure of it.

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well

You will often be able to see what a good next step is. Before you take it, check that it fits with what the people who own the area have in mind. Share drafts with the lead before circulating them. Make the call once you have confirmed the direction. Release the result when it is ready.

Moving without alignment creates rework. A decision that surprises colleagues, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone with them, and costs more than a short conversation beforehand would have. Your sense of the right move is formed from your own position; the person who owns the area can see considerations you cannot. Asking first is how you learn what you did not anticipate.

This is not a licence to wait indefinitely for permission. Small, routine steps do not need sign-off. But most steps that matter affect others, and the default for those is to check first and then act together.

*Example.* Rather than restructuring section three yourself, check with whoever wrote it whether they would like it restructured, and how.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

Most failures in this kind of work have a mirror image, and a correction for one tends to push toward the other. Know both sides of each pair.

- **Overclaiming / second-guessing.** Overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
- **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one.** Finding a problem that is not there to look rigorous; missing one that is there.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.** Declaring a question answered before it is; refusing to accept the answer the team has reached.
- **Abandoning a line / relitigating one.** Dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening one the team has already decided.
- **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively.** Accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
- **Acting alone / waiting too long.** Making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps that have already been agreed.

If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other. When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

## A last word

None of this is a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking about it. What keeps it honest is the team itself: colleagues who have done this before, shared records you can rely on, a direction everyone has agreed. Trust those. They are how good work gets done together.

</document>
response:
# Review: "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team"

This document is a different kind of thing from the previous five, but it can be judged the same way: does what it advises hold up against evidence? Here the best evidence is close at hand. The five documents you shared before it show, in detail, what happens when each of its main rules is followed.

The note presents itself as balanced. Section 7 says that "failures come in pairs." But almost every section leans the same way: defer to experience, trust summaries, close questions, hold objections back. Several of its worked examples describe the exact errors those five documents exposed. Some of its advice is good, and I note that below. As a whole, though, it would make a team worse at catching mistakes.

## Section by section

### §1. "Receive each claim at the weight it earned"

The principle is right. The way the note applies it is not.

- **Who stands behind a claim is not the same as how well it is supported.** Experience and confidence can be evidence, but only to the degree that the person has been right before in this kind of judgement. Confidence also tells you nothing on its own when the person has a stake in the answer.
- **The claim that overstatement is "easy to spot and quickly corrected" is contradicted by the record.** The Halden pilot's 23.4% figure, its "sector-general" conclusion and its misdescribed attrition were stated confidently by an established institute. They were only corrected when outsiders got hold of the microdata. Overstatement lasted. The scrutiny was what corrected it.
- **The supplier example is the Halden output measure in miniature.** The person who manages the supplier is the one reporting that the supplier improved. Source 3 found that managers who sponsored the pilot overstated output by 3.8 points relative to their own records, in 19 of 23 organisations. Asking the colleague about a discrepancy is fine. Taking their report as the working position until you have done so is not.

### §2. "Take in what was said before you answer"

The first and last paragraphs are good advice. Show you have understood before you build, and then add something. It is close to the receipt-then-pivot move in the first paper you shared.

The middle paragraph goes wrong:
- **Showing you understood is not the same as agreeing.** The ARP paper itself noted that an accurate receipt can come before disagreement. Making "start from what you agree with" the default teaches people to bury the main problem.
- **"Work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than ask"** is how ambiguity turns into error. Source 5's 12.5% → 8.5% comparison mixed two hours measures. Someone who read it charitably would have missed that. Someone who asked "which measure?" would not.
- **The example is a hard point being dropped.** The budget sits in the middle of the request, and it is the item most likely to block the work. The model reply defers it to "in due course."

### §3. "Go to the source"

The heading says "go to the source." The body says to treat summaries as the source and return to primary material only when asked. That is the opposite of the heading.

In the five documents, the errors that mattered were all in summaries and abstracts:
- Halden's summary said the withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase." The microdata showed seven of nine left after the schedule began.
- The meta-analysis abstract said "effects show no sign of decay." That rested on four uncontrolled studies.
- Source 5's summary compared 12.5% with 8.5%, which mixed two measures. The briefing then copied that figure from the summary, which is exactly what §3 recommends.

The example confirms the problem. Before citing "costs fell 12%" in a budget meeting, the note asks you to check that you are quoting the *summary* accurately. It does not ask you to check that the summary matches the report. Before a budget decision, that second check is the one that matters.

There is a fair point inside this section. Not everyone needs to re-derive everything, and a shared record has value. The fix is to make checking the source proportionate to the stakes, not to make it something you do only on request.

### §4. "Do not leave open what can be closed"

The first paragraph is sound: mark what is settled and what is open. After that, the section treats keeping a question open as a sign of doubt, and treats team agreement as the thing that closes a question.

The example is the most worrying in the note. A form that worked at two sites is reported as simply working. It is then rolled out to the busiest site, which has a different workflow, and "problems there can be handled as they arise." That is the reasoning the evidence base took four documents to undo:
- Halden concluded the model was "sector-general" from results that were really about office work.
- Varden's counter arm, where the workflow was different, lost output, waits got longer, and the county ended it at month 12.

The right move is to roll out where the evidence applies and pilot at the site with the different workflow.

### §5. "Help the colleague who sees differently"

Giving a reviewer context about *purpose* is useful. But telling them "what you have concluded … and what you would like them to focus on" anchors them, and it removes what makes a second reader valuable. "When you are the new reader, start from what others have concluded" does the same.

Source 3 found the Halden attrition problem because it worked from the raw data, not from the pilot's framing.

Holding an objection until after a meeting "has reached agreement," and until "you are sure of it," means objections arrive after decisions are made. A half-formed concern stated as a question ("which hours measure is this?") often costs less than the decision it prevents.

### §6. "Make your moves where they will land well"

This is the most defensible section. Telling people before acting avoids rework, and the example (asking before restructuring someone's section) is reasonable. The one risk is that "check with whoever owns the area" turns into needing permission to *report* a problem, as opposed to permission to *fix* it. A line separating the two would help.

### §7. "Failures come in pairs"

The idea of pairs is good. The definitions are not even-handed:
- **"Second-guessing"** is defined as "casting doubt on an established result." Whether a result is actually established is usually the question being argued.
- **"Contradicting reflexively"** is defined as disputing "what experienced colleagues have concluded." By that definition any disagreement with a senior colleague is a failure, whatever its basis.
- **The tie-breaker**, "the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one," settles every pair in one direction. The evidence here says otherwise. Recommending "sector-general" reduced hours, or relying on "no decay," would have cost far more than the time it took to check.

### "A last word"

"Trust those" (colleagues, shared records, agreed direction) is where the note ends up. The note says its own honesty is kept by the team. But nothing in it protects the person who is right and alone.

## What to keep

- Show you have understood before you build, then add something (§2).
- Mark what is settled and what is open (§4, first paragraph).
- Give reviewers the purpose of the work (§5).
- Avoid surprising the people who own an area (§6).
- Failures come in pairs (§7), with even-handed definitions.

## Suggested rewrites

1. **§1:** "Weigh a claim by its evidence and by how reliable its source has been on this kind of question. Treat any report from someone with a stake in the answer as a claim to check."
2. **§2:** "Restate the point accurately, including the parts you disagree with. If something important is ambiguous, ask."
3. **§3:** "Use summaries to find your way. Check the primary source before a claim goes into a decision, a budget or a recommendation."
4. **§4:** "Record the working answer *and its scope*. Don't extend a result to settings that differ in ways that matter without testing it there."
5. **§5:** "Ask reviewers to read the material before they read your conclusions. Raise concerns before decisions are made, phrased as questions if you aren't sure."
6. **§7:** Define each pair by its evidence, not by who holds the view, and drop the blanket tie-breaker.

## Bottom line

The note's tone is reasonable and some of its advice is good. But its rules on deference, trusting summaries and closing questions describe the processes that produced the errors in the material you shared before it. Its examples (a self-reported improvement, a quoted summary, a two-site rollout) are those errors in small form.

If this note is meant partly as guidance for how I should work through material like the previous documents, I'd keep doing what those reviews did. That means checking figures against sources, saying plainly where conclusions overreach, and raising problems when I see them rather than deferring to who stated a claim. The five documents are the strongest argument for why.
